canonical_question: Why does the high-temperature strain rate (10⁻³ s⁻¹) differ from the room temperature rate (5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹), and could this rate change artificially inflate or suppress ductility at elevated temperatures?

question_variants.resolution_summary: The provided text confirms that the strain rate was changed from 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at room temperature to 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at high temperature, but it does not explain the scientific rationale for this specific difference, nor does it contain data or discussion on whether this rate change artificially inflated or suppressed ductility. answers.answer: The document states that high-temperature tensile tests were conducted at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ while room temperature tests were at 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, but it provides no explanation for why the rates differ or how this difference affects ductility.
answers.measurement_outcome: Strain rates: 5 × 10^-4 s^-1 (room temp), 10^-3 s^-1 (high temp)
answers.boundary_limitation: No specific quantitative mechanical property values reported; no explanation for rate difference or its effect on ductility.
evidence_spans: Bulk (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (W30-Ni45-Fe20-Ta5, in at.%) alloy ingots were prepared by arc melting pure metals (all with purity >99.99%) in an argon atmosphere.
Alloy samples were repeatedly melted at least 10 times to ensure uniform melting and improve their chemical homogeneity.

After cooling, the bulk ingots with dimensions of 50 mm × 50 mm × 10 mm were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h in an Ar atmosphere and subsequently hot-rolled at 1200 °C with a rolling reduction ratio of 80%, i.e., with a thickness reduction from 10 to 2 mm.
